props.title: Speed 2: Cruise Control
props.initialSlug: Buckle up, the sea's on fire!

sections.content: Speed 2: Cruise Control (1997) stands as one of Hollywood's most notorious sequel misfires, attempting to replicate the tight thrills of Speed (1994) but stumbling dramatically. Where the original confined its action to a bus that couldn't slow down, creating genuine tension through spatial limitations, the sequel's cruise ship setting proved paradoxically both too large and too slow. Sandra Bullock returns but Keanu Reeves wisely opted out, replaced by Jason Patric in a performance that lacks the magnetic urgency Reeves brought to the original. The film exemplifies the "bigger isn't better" lesson that plagued many 90s action sequels like Batman & Robin (1997) and Lost World: Jurassic Park (1997).

sections.content: The late 90s marked a turning point for action cinema, as practical effects-driven films like Speed (1994) gave way to CGI-heavy spectacles. Speed 2 (1997) awkwardly straddles this transition, attempting to blend practical stunts with unconvincing computer effects, particularly in its infamous cargo ship crash finale. The film's $160 million budget - massive for 1997 - yielded none of the white-knuckle intensity of its predecessor, which cost less than half as much. This parallels similar big-budget action disappointments of the era like Waterworld (1995) and Cutthroat Island (1995).

Director Jan de Bont, who had successfully helmed both Speed (1994) and Twister (1996), seemed to lose his grasp on action geography and pacing. The cruise ship's massive scale diffuses tension rather than concentrates it. Willem Dafoe's villain, a disgruntled computer engineer seeking revenge, lacks the menacing simplicity of Dennis Hopper's mad bomber from the original. The film's failure marked the end of the "Die Hard on a..." formula that had dominated 90s action cinema since Under Siege (1992) and Passenger 57 (1992). SUBHEAD: The Death of the Pure Action Thriller

movies.title: Die Hard
movies.slug: The definitive confined-space action thriller that launched countless imitators. Bruce Willis's everyman hero battles terrorists in a Los Angeles skyscraper.

sections.content: Speed 2 (1997)'s commercial and critical failure helped signal the end of the pure action thriller era. The genre would soon evolve toward either effects-heavy superhero spectacles like X-Men (2000) or grittier, more grounded fare like The Bourne Identity (2002). The film's issues highlight why contained action works better with limited scope - compare it to later successful confined thrillers like Phone Booth (2002) or Buried (2010).
